panels.rationale: Single H&E histology panel from an article on intestinal-type adenocarcinoma, captioned as solid subtype of intestinal-type adenocarcinoma. The caption and in-text mention identify it as a real patient tumor with solid growth and minor poorly differentiated glandular lumina, matching gastric adenocarcinoma intestinal type. No skin or ethnicity information is provided. [raw subtype: solid]

panels.figure_caption: Intestinal-type adenocarcinoma, solid subtype. The tumor displays a diffuse growth pattern with minor amounts of poorly differentiated glandular lumina. There is high mitotic activity. H–E stain ×250
in_text_mentions: Intra- and extracellular mucins and few goblet cells may be seen. ITACs of the colonic subtype often show extensive invasive growth. Solid subtype of ITAC is less differentiated and features predominantly solid growth patterns with minor amounts of glandular structures (Fig. 3). Mucinous subtype of ITAC displays distended glands or cell clusters within pools of extracellular mucin (Fig. 4). Cells of signet-ring type may be seen. Mucinous ITACs resemble the mucinous variant of colorectal adenocarcinoma. Mixed subtype of ITAC contains different compositions of the various growth patterns above.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A is a real patient histology image showing invasive gastric adenocarcinoma (intestinal type) within the submucosa, beneath the muscularis mucosae, with overlying normal gastric mucosa. The caption and article confirm the target disease. B: Panel B is a real patient higher-power histology image of invasive gastric adenocarcinoma (intestinal type) showing cribriform glandular architecture, marked cytological atypia, anisokaryosis, loss of nuclear polarity, and intraluminal necrosis, consistent with the target disease.
panels.attribution_text: Essadi et al. Invasive Gastric Adenocarcinoma Arising in a Giant Pedunculated Polyp Causing Intermittent Gastric Outlet Obstruction: A Case Report. Cureus None. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 11.
panels.figure_caption: Higher-magnification histological assessment of the invasive component. (A) Intermediate-power view demonstrating invasive adenocarcinoma within the submucosa (yellow star), beneath the muscularis mucosae (red star), with the overlying normal gastric mucosa indicated by the green star, ×10. (B) Higher-power view of the invasive adenocarcinoma showing cribriform glandular architecture (red arrows), marked cytological atypia and anisokaryosis (orange arrow), loss of nuclear polarity (blue arrow), and intraluminal necrosis (green arrow), ×20. Hematoxylin, eosin, and saffron staining.
in_text_mentions: The carcinoma extended through the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa, with a maximum depth of invasion of 2,400 μm. The invasive focus within the polyp stalk measured 1,360 μm in greatest dimension. The deep resection margin was free of tumor, with a minimum clearance of 3 mm from the invasive carcinoma (Figures 10-11). These findings, including the measurements of invasion depth, were confirmed on a second histopathological review.

Her hemoglobin improved to 9.7 g/dL, and she was discharged with magnesium hydroxide and omeprazole. She returned to our facility for a scheduled EUS with EDGE procedure for staging, approximately one week later. During the second EUS with EDGE, there was visualization of the Roux-en-Y and preexisting AXIOS stent placement with healthy-appearing mucosa and an obstructing (about 80%) gastric antral mass. There was sonographic evidence of invasion in the muscularis propria manifested by abutment (Figure 3).

in_text_mentions: ss, with pathology revealing intramucosal adenocarcinoma with human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) immunohistochemical stain positive. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial contrast-enhanced CT shows an enhancing perigastric/greater curvature lymph node, consistent with locoregional nodal spread of gastric adenocarcinoma. B: Axial contrast-enhanced CT shows enhancing infrapyloric lymph nodes, consistent with regional nodal spread of gastric adenocarcinoma. C: Axial contrast-enhanced CT shows enhancing celiac lymph nodes as part of lymph nodal spread from gastric adenocarcinoma. D: Axial contrast-enhanced CT shows enhancing para-aortic lymph nodes, consistent with metastatic nodal spread of gastric adenocarcinoma.

The circumferential thickening of the pylorus and duodenum with perigastric lymphadenopathy favored gastric malignancy over a periampullary tumor. plate_findings.evidence: thickened stomach wall

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial contrast-enhanced CT in a patient with resectable gastric adenocarcinoma shows thickened stomach wall along the lesser curvature, with manual GTV contour annotation. B: Axial contrast-enhanced CT in a patient with unresectable gastric adenocarcinoma shows thickened gastric wall with manual GTV contour annotation.
panels.attribution_text: Yu et al. A quantitative model based on gross tumor volume of gastric adenocarcinoma corresponding to N-stage measured at multidetector computed tomography for preoperative determination of resectability: A case control study.. Frontiers in oncology 2022. doi:10.3389/fonc.2022.1001593. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: (A) In a 61-year-old male with resectable gastric adenocarcinoma, the initial preoperative abdominal contrast-enhanced computed tomography scans depict the gross tumor volume (GTV) obtained by manual sketching along the margin of the lesser curvature of the thickened stomach wall slice-by-slice, and the GTV is 9.94 cm3. (B) The transverse contrast-enhanced computed tomography scans in a 62-year-old female with unresectable gastric adenocarcinoma with lung metastasis show that the tumor area is manually drawn along the margin of the thickened gastric wall, and the GTV is 39.10 cm3.
in_text_mentions: thickening of stomach wall, so we selected the portal venous phase images to measure GTV. The contour of the GA focus was manually drawn along the visible margins of the tumor, avoiding air, water and stomach contents ( Figure 1 ), and then the software automatically calculated the tumor area. The above analysis was repeated for each contiguous transverse sections until the whole tumor was covered on axial CT images. When it was difficult to accurately sketch along the contours of tumors based on the axial CT data, we obtained a coronal or sagittal reconstruction image for better delineation.

The part of 0-IIa showed a partially absent microsurface pattern partially with white opaque substance and a fine network of irregular microvessels (C).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A is H&E histology of a 0-I lesion explicitly called gastric intestinal-type adenocarcinoma in the in-text mention; it shows irregular glandular/tubular formation and low-grade nuclear atypia. B: Panel B is H&E histology of a well-differentiated gastric adenocarcinoma with low-grade atypia and tubular structure; this is compatible with the configured intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma, although the caption does not repeat the intestinal-type designation for this panel.
panels.attribution_text: Takahashi et al. Inverted gastric adenocarcinoma of fundic gland mucosa type colliding with well differentiated adenocarcinoma: A case report.. Medicine 2017. doi:10.1097/md.0000000000007080. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Histological findings. The 0-I lesion was gastric adenocarcinoma composed of columnar cells with low-grade atypia, 3 mm in size (A). The superficial part of the 0-I lesion consisted of a papillary structure mimicking foveolar epithelium with upward growth. The deeper part consisted of a tubular structure resembling the fundic gland showing inverted downward growth to the submucosal layer with the lamina muscularis mucosae. The 0-IIa lesion was well differentiated adenocarcinoma with low-grade atypia, 15 mm in size (B).
in_text_mentions: The histological findings differed between the 0-I lesion and the 0-IIa lesion. The 0-I lesion was gastric intestinal-type adenocarcinoma (Fig. 3A). The deeper part consisted of a tubular structure resembling the fundic gland that showed inverted downward growth to the submucosal layer with the lamina muscularis mucosae. The 0-I lesion was diagnosed as papillary adenocarcinoma-well-differentiated tubular adenocarcinoma. The 0-IIa lesion was composed of a tubular structure

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Enhanced CT panel from a patient with gastric adenocarcinoma shows the lesser-curvature gastric fundus lesion and enlarged regional lymph nodes, matching captioned/in-text manifestations. B: H&E histology panel confirms moderately to poorly differentiated gastric adenocarcinoma with irregular glandular architecture, consistent with the configured gastric adenocarcinoma intestinal-type target. [raw subtype: intestinal_type] C: Immunohistochemistry panel shows CK8/18-positive tumor cells from the same gastric adenocarcinoma case; this supports the diagnosis but is a nonspecific epithelial marker rather than a distinct morphologic finding.

in_text_mentions: e lesion site appeared rough, with significant and homogeneous enhancement on the contrast-enhanced scan. Multiple mildly enhanced lymph nodes were observed in the hepatogastric space, with the largest measuring 1.4 cm in short diameter. The imaging diagnosis indicated a space-occupying lesion on the lesser curvature of the gastric fundus with multiple enlarged lymph nodes (Figure 1A). Routine gastroscopy demonstrated a protruding lesion at the same site, and biopsy pathology confirmed moderately to poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma (Figure 1B) with positive staining for CK8/18 (Figure 1C).

B: Middle radial endoscopic ultrasound frame labeled 'Gastric body mass' with an arrow pointing to a hypoechoic heterogeneous mass, matching the caption describing a mass in the gastric body/antrum invading the muscularis propria and serosa in a patient with a distal gastric mass highly suspicious for adenocarcinoma. findings.evidence: marked nuclear atypia with nuclear enlargement

panels.rationale: H&E/Saffron high-power micrograph of the gastric polyp's adenomatous component showing high-grade dysplasia with cribriform glandular architecture, nuclear atypia and prominent nucleoli (arrowed). This is the intestinal-type glandular neoplastic proliferation described in the case of invasive gastric adenocarcinoma arising in the polyp; it is a dysplastic precursor of the invasive tumor, hence moderate confidence.
panels.attribution_text: Essadi et al. Invasive Gastric Adenocarcinoma Arising in a Giant Pedunculated Polyp Causing Intermittent Gastric Outlet Obstruction: A Case Report. Cureus None. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 7.
panels.figure_caption: High-power histological view showing high-grade dysplasia within the adenomatous component, characterized by complex glandular crowding and cribriform architecture (red arrows), intraluminal necrosis (green arrow), loss of cell polarity (blue arrow), and marked nuclear atypia with nuclear enlargement and prominent nucleoli (orange arrow). Hematoxylin, eosin, and saffron staining, ×20.
in_text_mentions: Histopathological examination of the polypectomy specimen revealed a tubular adenoma containing low-grade dysplasia in approximately 20% of the lesion and high-grade dysplasia in approximately 80% (Figure 7), with an associated moderately differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma (Figures 8-9).

panels.rationale: Single endoscopic image from a case report titled 'Exuberant squamous metaplasia of the gastric mucosa in a patient with gastric adenocarcinoma.' The in-text description states endoscopy showed an irregular depressed hyperemic lesion covered with a whitish plaque on the cardia, and biopsy revealed infiltrating neoplastic single cells. The panel is a real patient endoscopic image showing the gastric adenocarcinoma lesion; the irregular depressed hyperemic mucosal lesion is best captured by the vocabulary term for irregular nodular mucosa/mucosal irregularity. The whitish plaque and white mucosa are proposed findings because no exact vocabulary term is provided.
panels.attribution_text: Ahn et al. Exuberant squamous metaplasia of the gastric mucosa in a patient with gastric adenocarcinoma.. Diagnostic pathology 2015. doi:10.1186/s13000-015-0281-5. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Endoscopic findings of the stomach. An area of white mucosa was found in the cardia contiguous to the esophageal mucosa. On the edge of this area, an irregular and slightly depressed hyperemic lesion was observed.

The lesion was approximately 4 cm in diameter and the whitish plaque was partly contiguous with the esophageal mucosa at the gastroesophageal junction. The biopsy specimen revealed infiltrating neoplastic single cells with benign squamous epithelium (Figure 2). panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: White-light endoscopic view of the gastric lesion in a patient whose lesion was diagnosed as cancer by histopathology and whose article is indexed to gastric adenocarcinoma; the elevated yellowish granular lesion is the malignant tumor. The specific reported subtype (foveolar/mucous neck cell-mixed adenocarcinoma) differs from intestinal type, so attribution rests on the configured disease key and histopathologic diagnosis. B: Narrow-band imaging of the same histologically confirmed adenocarcinoma, with the lesion extent outlined by a yellow dotted line; shows the demarcated brownish granular tumor area. C: Magnifying NBI image of the histologically proven gastric adenocarcinoma, demonstrating abnormal microsurface and microvascular architecture. D: Acetic acid chromoendoscopy of the same histologically confirmed gastric adenocarcinoma, highlighting the granular tumor microsurface.

The caption and in-text mentions explicitly state this is a metastatic deposit from gastric adenocarcinoma, supporting attribution to the configured gastric adenocarcinoma intestinal type. The panel is an endoscopic patient image of the colonic mucosa, but the visible abnormality (friable submucosal infiltrative mass-like thickening with luminal narrowing) is only partially captured by the provided gastric-oriented endoscopy vocabulary, hence a modest confidence and proposed findings for the unmatched features. No skin, nails, lips or oral mucosa are shown, so skin tone is null; age and ethnicity are not stated.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Contrast-enhanced CT panel from a case of gastric adenocarcinoma showing gastric body wall thickening/enhancement and bulky lymph node swelling, directly matching target disease CT findings. B: Contrast-enhanced CT panel showing hepatic lesions with central necrosis and heterogeneous enhancement in a patient with gastric adenocarcinoma and synchronous liver metastases; attributed via article title and caption context. C: Early-phase contrast-enhanced CT panel showing a hepatic metastasis with heterogeneous enhancement in a patient with gastric adenocarcinoma and multiple liver metastases. D: Late-phase contrast-enhanced CT panel showing a hepatic metastasis with washout in a patient with gastric adenocarcinoma and multiple liver metastases. E: Late-phase contrast-enhanced CT panel showing a hepatic metastasis with washout in a patient with gastric adenocarcinoma and multiple liver metastases.

in_text_mentions: 185 U/mL (normal: <37 U/mL). Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed thickening and enhancement of the gastric body wall, bulky lymph node swelling, and five bilobar hepatic lesions, the largest measuring 60 mm with central necrosis and heterogeneous enhancement. All liver tumors exhibited hyperattenuation in the arterial phase and washout in the venous phase. The liver surface was smooth, the liver edge was sharp, and no epigastric venous dilatation was observed (Fig. 1). Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a 50- × 40-mm type 2 tumor at the greater curvature of the gastric body.

in_text_mentions: F-18 FDG PET/CT showed gastric antral wall thickening with slightly increased but indistinct FDG uptake compared with the liver, with an SUVmax of 7.3 (Figure 2). No distant abnormal tracer uptake suggestive of metastatic disease was identified.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (MUC5AC, MUC2, MUC6, Ki-67). MUC5AC: Real patient immunohistochemistry panel of the gastric tumour, labelled MUC5AC. The caption states the tumour cells are positive for MUC5AC, and the image shows strong cytoplasmic staining of the neoplastic glandular epithelium with tubular/glandular architecture. Note the case was finally diagnosed as foveolar-type gastric adenocarcinoma (MUC5AC+/MUC2−/MUC6−), i.e. a gastric rather than intestinal immunophenotype, so attribution to the configured intestinal-type key is only partially supported; confidence therefore limited. MUC2: Same patient's tumour stained for MUC2; the caption reports negativity, and the section shows glandular tumour architecture without MUC2 expression. Negative staining for the intestinal marker argues against intestinal-type differentiation, so this panel's support for the configured intestinal-type disease key is weak. MUC6: Patient tumour stained for MUC6; the caption states the tumour...

panels.figure_caption: Immunohistochemistry findings. The tumor cells are positive for MUC5AC and negative for MUC2 and MUC6. Ki‐67 labeling is observed on the surface of the lesion.
in_text_mentions: lesion consisted of tubular adenocarcinoma in the surface layer (Figure 3a–c), manifesting cystic dilation of the fundic glands and hyperplasia of the foveolar epithelium (Figure 3d). Immunohistochemically, the tumor cells were positive for MUC5AC but negative for MUC2 and MUC6. Ki‐67 overexpression was observed in almost all tumor cells (Figure 4). The tumor cells were also negative for pepsinogen I and H+/K+ ATPase. The final pathological diagnosis was FTGA. The esophagogastroduodenoscopy performed 1 year after the ESD revealed no recurrence of gastric cancer or multiple hyperplastic polyps.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Panel a is a real patient endoscopic image showing a protruding, hemi-circumferential pyloric tumor causing luminal narrowing (asterisk), matching the caption and the case's confirmed gastric adenocarcinoma. The tumor surface is irregular/nodular; the protruding mass itself is best matched to the irregular nodular mucosa finding in the provided vocabulary. b: Panel b is a real patient endoscopic image of the same pyloric mass showing a clearly ulcerated, necrotic tumor surface indicated by the arrow, consistent with a fungating ulcerated gastric adenocarcinoma at endoscopy.

panels.figure_caption: Endoscopic examination reveals a protruding and hemi-circumferential tumor of the gastric pylorus causing narrowing of the lumen (asterisk) (a), with an ulcerated surface (arrow) (b).
in_text_mentions: This is the case of a 64-year-old patient who presented with epigastric pain and vomiting for the past two months prior to consultation. The patient had no relevant medical history and did not report any other general symptoms. Physical examination revealed a tenderness in the epigastric region with no evident palpable mass. Endoscopic examination showed a polypoid mass measuring approximately 7×4.5 cm with a bulging and ulcerated surface located at the pyloric region (Figure 1).

in_text_mentions: of the posterior wall of the stomach at the tumor site, and distal gastrectomy with combined resection of the anterior lobe of the transverse mesentery was performed. The reconstruction was performed using the Roux-en-Y technique. The operation time was 226 minutes, and the blood loss was 500 mL. On the 30th postoperative day, the patient was discharged home. In surgical specimens, type 3 lesions of 45×45 mm in the lower gastric region and 35 mm of type 0-IIa tumors (Paris classification) were found on the oral side of the type 3 lesions, but they were not detected preoperatively (Figure 2a).

The immunostainings were negative in the area of type 0-IIa lesions. No mixture of ductal adenocarcinoma components was observed in the area of the type 3 lesions. Sectioning and mapping of the specimen at the border of both lesions revealed that the ductal adenocarcinoma and GACED lesions were located adjacent to each other (Figure 2b). At the border between the two lesions, the ductal adenocarcinoma lesion was superficial, whereas the GACED lesion was located deep (Figure 5).

panels.figure_caption: Pathohistological images of the resected specimen. Low-power field (A) and high-power field (B–D) images of hematoxylin and eosin-stained specimens. The scale bars represent 800 μm (A), 200 μm (B), 40 μm (C, D), and 100 μm (E). The blue arrows show the boundaries of the tumor (A). The blue frame indicates the lesion’s superficial dense tubular and papillary structures and deeper pyloric gland-like glandular ducts (B). The tumor cells were similar to foveolar epithelium (C) and pyloric gland cells (D) with low-grade cell atypia and obvious architectural atypia. A lymphovascular invasion was visible (indicated by the black arrow) (E).

in_text_mentions: Multiple biopsies were performed. Histologically, the tumor is organized in multiple tubules and papillae, with evident fibrovascular cores (Figure 2a, 2b). The tumor cells are cuboidal to columnar with evident cytonuclear atypia presenting as enlarged, atypical nuclei, with fine chromatin and prominent nucleoli. The cytoplasm is abundant and often has a clear appearance (Figure 2e, 2f). Immunohistochemical analysis showed positivity of tumor cells for CK7 and partial positivity for cyclin D1 but no expression of CK20 and CD10, which was helpful in excluding a potential renal origin.

Additionally, the tumor shows abundant intraluminal eosinophilic secretions (Figure 2c, 2d, asterisk), which gave the tumor a remarkable morphological resemblance to thyroid carcinoma. Immunohistochemical staining for TTF1 and thyroglobulin was negative, allowing the exclusion of a thyroid origin. Therefore, the diagnosis of a clear cell papillary adenocarcinoma of the stomach was established.

in_text_mentions: Intra- and extracellular mucins and few goblet cells may be seen. ITACs of the colonic subtype often show extensive invasive growth. Solid subtype of ITAC is less differentiated and features predominantly solid growth patterns with minor amounts of glandular structures (Fig. 3). Mucinous subtype of ITAC displays distended glands or cell clusters within pools of extracellular mucin (Fig. 4). Cells of signet-ring type may be seen. Mucinous ITACs resemble the mucinous variant of colorectal adenocarcinoma. Mixed subtype of ITAC contains different compositions of the various growth patterns above.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: H&E histology of duodenal submucosa shows focal glandular architecture of a poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma in a patient with gastric adenocarcinoma; this supports the configured intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma, although the poorly differentiated/signet-cell component noted in the text lowers certainty. B: Higher-power H&E shows sheets of poorly differentiated carcinoma cells with pleomorphic nuclei and prominent nucleoli; compatible with gastric adenocarcinoma, but intestinal-type attribution is inferred from the article context and primary disease key.

in_text_mentions: Histopathology of the surgical specimen revealed a poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma along with few signet cells as well as focal glandular architecture (Figure 5). The adjacent mucosa showed the presence of tumor emboli. The malignant cells nested around the duodenal papilla. Since the tumor was unresectable, palliative chemotherapy was offered. However, the patient refused further active management and succumbed to her illness two months later.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A is a gastroscopic image from a patient with histologically confirmed gastric adenocarcinoma; caption and text describe type 0-IIa gastric tumors. The raised, irregular mucosal lesion corresponds to the vocabulary finding of irregular nodular mucosa. B: Panel B is H&E histology of one of the two biopsy-proven gastric adenocarcinomas, showing irregular glandular/tubular formations with atypical nuclei, consistent with intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma. C: Panel C is a second H&E field of the well-differentiated gastric adenocarcinoma, with irregular glandular architecture and nuclear atypia matching the histologic vocabulary for intestinal-type adenocarcinoma.
panels.attribution_text: Amano et al. Case report: Reversible brain atrophy with low titer anti-amphiphysin antibodies related to gastric adenocarcinoma.. Frontiers in neurology 2023. doi:10.3389/fneur.2023.1211814. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Gastroscopy and pathological findings. Two lesions of type 0-IIa gastric tumor (A). Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows two adenocarcinomas (B, C).
in_text_mentions: PH antibody is known as a paraneoplastic antineuronal antibody, we performed various tests to detect malignancy. Although colonoscopy and random skin biopsy showed normal findings, gastroscopy revealed type 0-IIa gastric tumors, and histological results suggested gastric adenocarcinomas with no evidence of metastasis (Figure 2A). After IVIg treatment (6 weeks after the initial high-dose methylprednisolone therapy), endoscopic submucosal dissection was performed and the tumors were completely removed. in_text_mentions: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) revealed a 110-mm-sized exophytic gastric tumor (Figure 1a, 1b).

The gastric wall adjacent to the exophytic gastric tumor was discontinuous; however, the continuity of the gastric intraluminal surface was maintained (Figure 1a). in_text_mentions: A baseline EGD performed two weeks after discharge, in accordance with contemporary guidelines recommending evaluation for gastric malignancy in patients with PA [7], revealed a 30-mm semi-pedunculated polyp at the incisura with spontaneous bleeding (Figure 4). panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (a, b, c, d, e). a: Clinical photo of an erythematous, indurated neck plaque in a case of metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma to the cutaneous neck/chest wall; cutaneous metastasis is a less common manifestation of the target disease. b: Clinical photo of an erythematous, indurated plaque involving the neck and anterior chest in metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma; this is a recognized but uncommon cutaneous metastasis presentation. c: CT shows enhancement and thickening of the anterior neck, corresponding to metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma involvement in a disease-focused article about cutaneous/soft tissue metastasis. d: H&E section demonstrates a pleomorphic dermal infiltrate in the patient's cutaneous metastasis from gastric adenocarcinoma; the panel is part of a case-confirmed metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma figure. e: Higher-power H&E shows pleomorphic dermal infiltrate with cytoplasmic mucin interpreted as consistent with gastric...

panels.figure_caption: (a and b) Front and side views of erythematous, indurated plaque on neck and anterior chest. (c) Enhancement and thickening of anterior neck on CT imaging. in_text_mentions: s notable for marked skin thickening of the anterior neck and sclerotic foci in several bones. A punch biopsy showed a dermal infiltrate composed of CK7, CDX2-positive tumor cells with cytoplasmic mucicarmine staining, most suggestive of metastatic adenocarcinoma from the upper gastrointestinal tract. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy confirmed the presence of a large submucosal gastric body mass, and the patient was diagnosed with stage IV metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma. Treatment with FOLFOX (leucovorin calcium (folinic acid), fluorouracil, and oxaliplatin) and nivolumab were started (Figure 1).

B: Panel B shows focal CK20 positivity in glandular structures from the same cervical lesion. It supports the glandular neoplastic process described in the article, but the exact fit to gastric adenocarcinoma intestinal type is limited because the reported entity is a gastric adenocarcinoma of the cervix.

in_text_mentions: howed glandular proliferation with a complex architectural pattern, lined by mucinous-type epithelium composed of tall cells with well-defined cytoplasmic borders, clear cytoplasm, and basally located nuclei with mild cytologic atypia. Goblet cells were present, with occasional mitotic figures (Figure 6). Immunohistochemically, the lesion was positive for CK7 and carbonic anhydrase IX (CAIX), with focal positivity for CK20 and PAX8 (Figure 7). MUC-6 was positive, and CEA showed apical staining. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (Left, Right). Left: H&E panel of a real patient open muscle biopsy showing poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma, which the article text states supports a diagnosis of gastric cancer metastases in skeletal muscle; the primary tumor is a poorly differentiated gastric adenocarcinoma (article title and in-text). Skeletal-muscle metastasis is a rare presentation, hence atypical. Attribution rests on the disease-focused article title plus the in-text statement that the histology established gastric cancer origin. Right: Immunohistochemistry panel from the same patient's muscle biopsy showing strong pan-cytokeratin positivity in the metastatic adenocarcinoma cells, confirming epithelial (gastric) origin as stated in the caption and in-text. No vocabulary finding matches IHC cytokeratin expression, so it is listed as a proposed finding.

panels.figure_caption: Histologic examination of the resected specimens with hematoxylin and eosin revealing moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. (a) From the stomach (magnification ×40), it shows the hypercellularity with basophilic, oligocytoplasmic, and pleomorphic cells and relatively large nuclei with dense chromatin and loose desmoplastic stroma which contains lymphocytic and plasmocytic infiltration. in_text_mentions: Pathology studies reported a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the stomach grade II with lymph node metastasis and peritoneal carcinomatosis (see Figure 2). The tumor infiltrates into the surrounding structures (T4b), there is metastasis in about 9 lymph nodes (N3), and there is no distant metastasis (M0) as shown in CT studies; these findings give stage IIIC to the tumor according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 7th edition.

Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a raised lesion with an irregular central ulcer on the anterior wall of the mid-gastric body (Fig. 2). The submucosal tumor appeared exposed in the lumen. The endoscopic findings were more suggestive of metastatic gastric tumors than of primary gastric cancer. A PET-CT scan revealed a right adrenal tumor.
